sentences: Adobe Max is the company’s annual creative conference that, in previous years, has come with a boatload of AI features.
The event gives us a peek at how the undisputed creative software industry leader is thinking about the future ( again: AI ).
This year may be a sentimental one for Adobe CEO Shantanu Narayen, as it will be his last in the top job.
Narayen announced this spring that he will be stepping down after 18 years as CEO, with customer experience chief Anil Chakravarthy slated to take over on Dec.
Adobe’s flagship programs, like Photoshop, have undergone major AI makeovers, including recent developments like AI audio and soundtrack generation .
This has been to the dismay of some of its creative customers who are wary of generative AI.
This year is expected to be no different.
But there are other tensions brewing, including Adobe’s $75 million settlement with the US Justice Department over subscription cancellations and new vibe-coded and free Adobe alternatives .
CNET is on the ground in Miami Beach, Florida, to bring you all the latest news.
Adobe Max officially kicks off on Tuesday, Nov.
You can follow along here for live updates and watch the presentation being livestreamed on YouTube.
A lot has changed since last year’s Adobe Max, but some things stay the same.
That is, Adobe is still all-in on artificial intelligence.
The biggest changes are the general release of AI assistants in Photoshop, Adobe Express and its AI hub, Firefly, first teased at last year’s conference.
These assistants are similar to chatbots, where you enter your request and the AI does the editing for you.
Adobe also released AI music generation tools and new photo editing modes .
For video editors, too, there are the new Premiere mobile apps .
Adobe tech is also now showing up in ChatGPT and Claude ; Disney is using Firefly to help design theme park rides .
And from what CNET has heard from Adobe execs , the company isn’t planning to slow down its AI research any time soon.
Other big Adobe news this year was the $75 million settlement Adobe and the US Department of Justice struck in March.
The case was brought by federal prosecutors over claims that Adobe made its subscriptions intentionally difficult to cancel.
Adobe denied any wrongdoing but agreed to pay $75 million to customers (in the form of free service) and another $75 million to the US government.
